items.prompt: Put the planets in order, starting with the one closest to the Sun.
hints: There are four small rocky planets, then four giant planets.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
Start with the smallest planet, which is the closest one to the Sun.
items.explanation: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. One way to remember it is: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming.

items.prompt: What causes day and night on Earth?

options.text: The Sun moves around the Earth every day.
options.why: The Sun only seems to move across the sky. It is the Earth that spins.

options.text: The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours.
The Moon blocks the Sun at night.
options.why: Night happens when your side of the Earth faces away from the Sun.

options.text: The Earth orbits the Sun once a day.
options.why: One orbit of the Sun takes a year, not a day.

hints: The Sun seems to move across the sky, but something else is really moving.
Think about which side of a spinning ball faces a lamp.
Cross out the choice that describes a whole year.
items.explanation: The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day, and the side facing away has night.

items.prompt: Why does the Moon seem to change shape during a month?

options.text: The Earth's shadow covers different parts of it.
options.why: The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which is rare.

options.text: Clouds cover parts of the Moon.
options.why: The phases happen on clear nights too.

options.text: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits the Earth.
The Moon really changes shape.
options.why: The Moon is always a ball. Only the part we see lit up changes.

hints: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon.
As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see it from different angles.
Picture a ball lit by a lamp while you walk around it. Watch how much of the lit half you see.
items.explanation: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half, from none at new moon to all of it at full moon.

items.prompt: Put the phases of the Moon in order, starting from new moon.
hints: Waxing means the lit part is growing. Waning means it is shrinking.
The Moon goes from no lit part, to half lit, to fully lit, then back again.
After new moon, the first thing you see is a thin, growing crescent.
items.explanation: From new moon, the lit part grows through crescent, first quarter and gibbous to full moon. Then it shrinks through gibbous, last quarter and crescent back to new moon, in about 29.5 days.

items.prompt: What causes the seasons in countries such as Japan and the United Kingdom?

options.text: The Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.
options.why: The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during winter in the north.

options.text: The Sun gives out more heat in summer.
options.why: The Sun gives out about the same energy all year.

options.text: The Moon blocks some sunlight in winter.
options.why: The Moon does not cause the seasons.

options.text: The Earth's axis is tilted as it orbits the Sun.

hints: The Earth's axis is not straight up. It leans to one side.
During the year, each half of the Earth leans towards the Sun and then away from it.
Think about which half of the Earth gets the Sun high in the sky and long days.
items.explanation: The Earth's axis is tilted. When your half of the Earth leans towards the Sun, the Sun is higher and days are longer, so it is summer. When it leans away, it is winter.

items.prompt: Indonesia is near the equator. Why does it have a rainy season and a dry season instead of a hot summer and a cold winter?

options.text: Near the equator the Sun is high all year, so it stays warm, and changing winds bring wet and dry seasons.
The equator is not tilted.
options.why: The whole Earth is tilted. Near the equator, the tilt changes the Sun's height only a little.

options.text: Indonesia is closer to the Sun than other countries.
options.why: Every country is about the same distance from the Sun.

options.text: Volcanoes make all the rain in Indonesia.
options.why: Rain comes from water vapour in the air, carried in by the winds.

hints: Near the equator, the Sun is high in the sky at midday all year round.
In Indonesia, the main winds change direction during the year.
Ask what keeps the temperature steady, then what brings the rain.
items.explanation: Near the equator, the Sun is high all year, so temperatures stay warm. Seasonal winds called monsoons bring wet air in one part of the year and drier air in another.

items.prompt: Sort the planets into rocky planets and giant planets.
hints: The four planets closest to the Sun are small and rocky.
The four outer planets are huge and made mostly of gas and ice.
Earth is a rocky planet. Start with its neighbours.
items.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small rocky planets. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant planets made mostly of gas and ice.

items.prompt: In 1610, Galileo Galilei used a telescope to see four small moons moving around Jupiter. Why was this important?

options.text: It proved that Jupiter is a star.
options.why: Jupiter is a planet. It shines by reflecting sunlight.

options.text: It showed that not everything in space moves around the Earth.
It showed that the Moon makes its own light.
options.why: Our Moon reflects sunlight, and this discovery was about Jupiter's moons.

options.text: It proved that the Earth is flat.
options.why: People knew the Earth was round long before Galileo.

hints: In 1610, many people believed that everything in the sky moved around the Earth.
Galileo saw moons circling a different planet.
Ask what these moons were moving around.
items.explanation: Jupiter's moons were moving around Jupiter, not around the Earth. This was evidence that the Earth is not the centre of everything, which supported the idea that the planets orbit the Sun.

items.prompt: Draw the Sun, the Earth and the Moon at the time of a full moon. Shade the half of the Moon that is lit by the Sun.

criteria.label: Places the Moon on the far side of the Earth from the Sun
Shades the half of the Moon that faces the Sun
Draws an arrow to show sunlight travelling from the Sun
Labels the Sun, the Earth and the Moon

hints: At full moon, we see the whole of the Moon's sunlit half.
Think about where the Moon must be for its lit side to face the Earth.
items.explanation: At full moon, the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun. Its sunlit half faces the Earth, so we see a whole bright disc.

items.prompt: Imagine the Earth's axis was not tilted at all. What would happen to the seasons in the United Kingdom?

options.text: There would be almost no seasons, and day length would barely change all year.
Summers would be much hotter.
options.why: Without a tilt, the Sun's midday height would stay the same all year, so there would be no hotter summer.

options.text: There would be two summers each year.
options.why: Seasons come from the tilt. With no tilt, there would be hardly any seasons at all.

options.text: There would be daylight for 24 hours every day.
options.why: The Earth would still spin, so there would still be day and night.

hints: Seasons happen because the tilt makes each half of the Earth lean towards and then away from the Sun.
Without a tilt, the Sun's path across the sky would be the same every day.
Ask what would change during the year if the Sun's height and day length stayed the same.
items.explanation: The tilt is what causes the seasons. With no tilt, the Sun would follow the same path every day, so day length and temperature would barely change during the year.

items.prompt: Label the Sun, the Earth and the Moon in this diagram.

figure.alt: Three round objects on a dark page. A very large yellow one is on the left. A medium blue one is in the lower middle. A very small grey one is at the upper right.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The Sun is by far the biggest object.
The Moon is the smallest and goes around the Earth.
items.explanation: The Sun is a huge star. The Earth is a planet. The Moon is a small rocky body that orbits the Earth.

items.prompt: The north end of the Earth's axis (N) always leans the same way. Tap the position where it is summer in the northern hemisphere.

figure.alt: A bright Sun in the middle with a circle around it. Three small Earths sit on the circle, one on the right, one on the left and one at the bottom. Each Earth has a tilted axis line marked N at the top, and all lean to the left.

hints: Summer happens in the hemisphere tilted towards the Sun.
Which way does each Earth lean compared with where the Sun is?
Find the Earth whose north end leans towards the Sun.
items.explanation: On the right the north end of the axis leans towards the Sun, so the northern hemisphere gets more direct sunlight and has summer.

items.prompt: How many planets orbit the Sun in our Solar System?
hints: Mercury is the closest to the Sun.
Neptune is the furthest planet.
Count: four rocky planets and four giant planets.
items.explanation: There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

items.prompt: The Earth spins once, a full turn of 360°, in 24 hours. Through how many degrees does it turn in 6 hours?
hints: The Earth spins at a steady rate.
6 hours is a fraction of 24 hours.
6 is one quarter of 24, so find one quarter of 360.
items.explanation: 6 hours is one quarter of a day. One quarter of 360° is 90°.

items.prompt: Jakarta clocks are 7 hours ahead of London. When it is 20:00 in Jakarta, what is the time in London in the 24-hour clock? Write only the hour, such as 5 for 05:00.
hints: Places further east see the Sun earlier, so their clocks are ahead.
London is behind Jakarta, so go back 7 hours.
Take 7 hours away from 20:00.
items.explanation: London is 7 hours behind, so 20:00 minus 7 hours is 13:00. The Earth spins, so places at different longitudes have different times.

items.caption: Daylight and season in the UK
items.prompt: Complete the table with the correct season in the UK.
head: Month
Daylight (hours)
Season
hints: The longest days come in the warmest season.
The shortest days come in the coldest season.
Look at 17 hours of daylight and 8 hours of daylight.
items.explanation: Long days with 17 hours of daylight mean summer. Short days with 8 hours of daylight mean winter.

items.caption: Seasons in two countries
items.prompt: When it is summer in the north, it is winter in the south. Complete the Australia column.
head: Month
UK season
Australia season
hints: The hemispheres have opposite seasons.
Use the June row as an example.
If the UK has winter, Australia has the season that is opposite it.
items.explanation: The northern and southern hemispheres lean towards the Sun at opposite times of the year, so their seasons are opposite.

items.prompt: How long does the Earth take to make one complete orbit around the Sun?

options.text: One day
options.why: One day is the time the Earth takes to spin once.

options.text: One month
options.why: A month is about the time the Moon takes to orbit the Earth.

options.text: One year
One week
options.why: A week is a unit of time we invented, not a movement in space.

hints: An orbit is a path around the Sun.
Which unit of time is based on the Earth going around the Sun?
It is the same period as the seasons repeating.
items.explanation: The Earth takes about 365 days, which is one year, to go once around the Sun.

items.prompt: Rangga says: "It is summer because the Earth is closer to the Sun." Which fact shows he is wrong?

options.text: The Sun is hotter in summer.
options.why: The Sun gives out the same heat all year.

options.text: When it is summer in the UK it is winter in Australia, but both are at the same distance from the Sun.
The Earth is always the same distance from the Sun.
options.why: The distance changes only slightly, and that is not why we have seasons.

options.text: The Moon is closer in summer.
options.why: The Moon does not cause seasons.

hints: If distance caused seasons, everyone would have summer together.
Think about two countries in different hemispheres.
What does Australia have when the UK has summer?
items.explanation: The two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time. Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis, not by distance from the Sun.

items.prompt: We always see the same side of the Moon from Earth. Why?

options.text: The Moon does not spin at all.
options.why: The Moon does spin, just slowly.

options.text: The Moon spins once in exactly the time it takes to orbit the Earth once.
The Earth blocks our view of the other side.
options.why: The Earth does not hide it. The Moon's spin matches its orbit.

options.text: The Moon is lit only on one side.
options.why: The Sun lights different parts as the Moon orbits.

hints: The Moon does spin on its axis.
Compare the time of one spin with the time of one orbit.
If both take the same time, which side faces Earth?
items.explanation: The Moon takes the same time to spin once as to orbit Earth once, so the same face always points towards us.

items.prompt: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon's shadow falls on part of the Earth. Where must the Moon be?

options.text: On the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun.
options.why: That arrangement makes the Earth's shadow fall on the Moon.

options.text: Between the Sun and the Earth.
Behind the Sun.
options.why: The Moon's shadow could not reach Earth from there.

options.text: Far from the Earth and the Sun.
options.why: To block the Sun it must line up between them.

hints: An eclipse needs the Sun, Moon and Earth in a line.
The Moon blocks the Sun's light.
The Moon must be in the middle of the line.
items.explanation: In a solar eclipse the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks sunlight from reaching part of the Earth.

items.prompt: Sort these objects into stars, planets and moons.
hints: A star makes its own light.
A planet orbits a star.
A moon orbits a planet.
items.explanation: The Sun is a star. Earth, Venus and Saturn orbit it, so they are planets. Our Moon and Europa orbit planets, so they are moons.

items.prompt: Put these in order of size, from the smallest to the largest.
hints: Planets are bigger than their moons.
The Sun is bigger than all the planets put together.
Jupiter is the largest planet.
items.explanation: The Moon is smaller than Earth. Jupiter is a giant planet much larger than Earth. The Sun is the largest by far.

items.prompt: Match each space word to its meaning.
pairs: spinning on an axis, once a day
the path around the Sun or a planet
the imaginary line through the poles
one orbit of the Earth around the Sun
hints: The Earth rotates while it orbits.
An axis is an imaginary line.
A year is about 365 days.
items.explanation: The Earth rotates on its axis once a day and orbits the Sun once a year.

items.prompt: Choose all the statements that are true.

options.text: The Sun is a star.
The Moon makes its own light.
The Earth is a planet that orbits the Sun.
Day and night are caused by the Earth spinning.

hints: Check each statement one at a time.
The Moon shines by reflecting light.
Three statements are true.
items.explanation: The Sun is a star and Earth is a planet that orbits it. Spinning gives day and night. The Moon only reflects sunlight.

items.prompt: The Moon shines because it ___ light from the Sun.
hints: The Moon is not a light source.
Light from the Sun hits it and then goes somewhere.
A mirror does the same thing to light.
items.explanation: The Moon does not make light. It reflects sunlight towards the Earth.

items.prompt: The Earth ___ on its axis once every 24 hours, which gives us day and night. It ___ the Sun once every year.
hints: One word is for spinning and one is for going around.
Day and night come from the spin.
The path around the Sun is called an orbit.
items.explanation: The Earth rotates once a day and orbits the Sun once a year.

items.prompt: In northern Norway the Sun does not set for weeks in June. Which idea explains this best?

options.text: Norway is closer to the Sun than other countries.
options.why: The distance to the Sun is almost the same for all places.

options.text: The Earth stops spinning in June.
options.why: The Earth never stops spinning.

options.text: The Moon reflects extra light onto Norway.
options.why: The Moon is too dim to do this.

options.text: In June the north is tilted towards the Sun, so places near the pole stay in sunlight as the Earth spins.

hints: Think about the tilt of the Earth's axis.
If a place is always in sunlight while spinning, it never gets night.
In June the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.
items.explanation: In June the north pole region is tilted towards the Sun. Places there stay in sunlight all through each spin, so the Sun does not set.
